function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

We can use the Open-Meteo API. We need to get forecast for NYC coordinates: latitude 40.7128, longitude -74.0060. We need daily temperature. The API: open-meteo.com. We can call the function requests_get with appropriate params. The function signature: url, headers optional, timeout, params: latitude, longitude, elevation optional. We need to specify the endpoint: "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast". We need query parameters: latitude, longitude, daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min, maybe also timezone. The function signature only includes latitude, longitude, elevation. But we can pass other query parameters? The function signature's params only includes latitude, longitude, elevation. It doesn't allow daily or timezone. So we cannot pass those. But maybe we can pass them as part of the URL? The function signature only includes params: latitude, longitude, elevation. So we can't pass daily. That seems limiting. But maybe the function signature is incomplete? The function signature says "params: {latitude?, longitude?, elevation?}". So we can't pass daily. But maybe we can pass them as part of the URL? The URL can include query string. But the function signature expects a URL string. We can embed query parameters in the URL string. So we can do: "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=40.7128&longitude=-74.0060&daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min&timezone=America/New_York". That would be fine. So we can call the function with that URL. The function will parse the URL and ignore the params field? Actually the function signature includes params separately. But we can pass the URL with query string. The function will still send GET request to that URL. The params field may be ignored. But we can set params empty. Then we parse the daily temperatures for next week. The user wants next week. We need to get forecast for next 7 days. The API returns daily arrays. We need to extract the next 7 days. The API returns daily.time array and daily.temperature_2m_max/min arrays. We need to find the dates for next week. We can compute current date. But we can just return the forecast for the next 7 days. The user didn't specify date range. So we can provide the forecast for the next 7 days. We'll parse the JSON and produce a summary.
